title: Assessing dietary supplement misinformation on popular Thai e-marketplaces: A cross-sectional content analysis
screen_reason: Cross-sectional content analysis of 332 dietary-supplement product web pages systematically selected from two popular Thai e-marketplaces in December 2022, reporting that 281 (84.6%) contained at least one 'misinformation' criterion, with per-criterion, per-platform and per-format breakdowns. Shares with clear denominators are present, so the paper is recorded. HOWEVER the construct is QUALITY, not CONTENT: the ground truth is Thai food-advertising REGULATION, not truth/falsity. The criteria include purely administrative non-compliance (L1 no FDA food serial number displayed; L2 serial number not valid in the FDA database; L3 no advertising licence number shown alongside a benefit description), and L3 alone accounts for 274 of the flags, i.e. it drives the headline 84.6%. A wholly truthful page can be flagged under L1-L3 (and under L8, which bans wording such as 'the best' or '100% safe'), which is the protocol's decisive test for QUALITY. The authors themselves state the construct is '(1) illegal food registration and (2) illegal advertising'. Rows are recorded with construct = QUALITY and borderline = true, i.e. kept but excluded from prevalence; under the QUALITY-ONLY screening rule this paper contributes no prevalence estimate.

estimates.platform: Two popular Thai e-marketplace (e-commerce) platforms, anonymised as platform A and platform B, identified from the 2020 Thailand Internet User Behaviour report
estimates.date: Sample web page URLs retrieved on 09 December 2022
estimates.measure_type: % of dietary-supplement product web pages violating at least one of ten Thai food-registration/advertising regulatory criteria (the paper's 'misinformation')
estimates.denominator: 332 dietary-supplement product web pages (164 from platform A across 5 subcategories; 168 from platform B across 14 subcategories), selected as every tenth page in each subcategory listing sorted by relevance
estimates.definition: The web page met at least one of the 10 modified CEWADS criteria (L1-L10): missing FDA food serial number; invalid serial number; benefit description without a displayed advertising licence number; healthcare-provider guarantee; claims of effects on body structure/organ function; claims to cure, relieve, treat or prevent disease; before/after images; prohibited wording ('the best', 'amazing', '100% safe'); claims of skin/beauty nourishment or weight loss; claims of sexual improvement. Duplicated violations on one page counted once.
estimates.misinfo_def: "Misinformation was defined broadly because, in public health, the focus is on health-related misinformation determined by various criteria. This study was concerned with the most serious context in Thailand, which was (1) illegal food registration and (2) illegal advertising."
estimates.source_quote: Out of the 332 DS web page samples, 281 web pages (84.6%) have at least one misinformation criterion. Five web pages (1.5%) have one criterion of misinformation, whereas 83 web pages (25.0%) have two criteria. The remaining 193 web pages (58.1%) have more than two criteria of misinformation [Figure 1].
estimates.page_loc: Results, 'The Overall Prevalence of Misinformation', p. 4
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Modified CEWADS criteria, originally developed by consensus of 21 Thai regulatory experts for consumer self-assessment and here refined/updated by three regulatory experts to the 2021 Thai FDA food-advertising rules; FDA serial numbers checked against the Thai FDA database. "Each criterion was evaluated for each DS web page sample by the researcher" - a single coder, with no inter-rater reliability, double coding or blinding reported. The authors note the FDA database is not always up to date, which "may result in the prevalence of problems being overestimated".
estimates.moderator_quote: This study systematically selected an equal number of web pages from each DS subcategory of each platform to ensure the comprehensive scope of DS claims. The two platforms have an unequal number of subcategories, (5 and 14), so the number per each subcategory varies by platform [Supplementary Table 1]. Every tenth web page in the list of each subcategory (sorted by most relevance) was included. The selected sample web pages' URLs were retrieved and collected on December 09, 2022.
estimates.notes: QUALITY, not CONTENT: the label is regulatory non-compliance, and the single largest contributor (L3, 274 pages, 82.5%) is a missing advertising-licence number, which says nothing about whether the page's claims are true. borderline = true. denom_selection = curated because the platform algorithm truncates category listings ('the researcher could not retrieve all DS web pages ... because of the restriction of the EM algorithm'). The abstract rounds this figure to 85%; the Results give 84.6%, used here.

estimates.notes: This is the single criterion closest to a health-falsity judgement (a dietary supplement claiming to treat hypertension or lower blood sugar), which is why it is recorded separately as a definition variant of the overall row. It is still coded QUALITY: the standard is legal permissibility of the claim, not verified falsity, and a claim with genuine evidence behind it would also be flagged. If an adjudicator decides that regulatory over-claiming of disease treatment counts as misleading health CONTENT, this 28.6% (and not the 84.6% headline) is the row to re-type. The quoted span is the Table 4 row as the PDF text renders it (criterion label, overall count 95, overall prevalence 28.6, platform A 36 (22.0), platform B 59 (35.1), p = 0.011).

missed_or_uncertain: The remaining per-criterion prevalences in Table 4 are recorded here rather than as rows (they are all the same country x platform x measure family, all QUALITY, and R4 favours a small number of well-characterised rows): L3 unapproved claims on food benefits 274 (82.5%) - platform A 138 (84.1%), B 136 (80.9%); L9 overclaims of skin/beauty nourishment, obesity or weight reduction 159 (47.9%) - A 87 (53.0%), B 72 (42.9%); L5 overclaims of influence on body structure/functions 140 (42.2%) - A 72 (43.9%), B 68 (40.5%); L6 95 (28.6%) [extracted]; L2 invalid FDA food serial number 84 (25.3%) - A 18 (11.0%), B 28 (16.7%); L10 overclaims of sexual improvement 54 (16.3%); L8 prohibited wording 51 (15.4%); L1 no FDA food serial number displayed 38 (11.4%); L7 before-after image 21 (6.3%); L4 healthcare-provider guarantee 4 (1.2%). By format (Table 5): text 208 (62.7%), image 201 (60.5%), video clip 19 (5.7%). By number of violated criteria (Figure 1 / text): 1 criterion 5 pages (1.5%), 2 criteria 83 (25.0%), more than 2 criteria 193 (58.1%). NOTE: L2's platform counts (18 + 28 = 46) do not sum to the stated overall 84, so the per-platform L2 figures appear to contain a reporting error; that is a further reason not to build rows on them. Figures cited from elsewhere and excluded by R8: the 70% pilot prevalence of illness-cure claims used for the sample-size calculation, the Thai FDA's withdrawal of over 200,000 web pages, the CRN survey (77%/84%/85% trust) and the 'one-third of weight loss claims ... adulterated' finding. Also not extracted: 354 pages were intended but only 332 obtained because the marketplaces delete pages.

rob.design: Cross-sectional content analysis (STROBE-reported, IRB COA NO.805/2022). Two Thai e-marketplaces selected from the 2020 ETDA Thailand Internet User Behaviour report; sample size 354 calculated from a 70% pilot prevalence with 5% precision plus 10% for dropout; every tenth web page in each dietary-supplement subcategory listing (sorted by relevance) was taken, equal numbers per subcategory, giving 164 pages from platform A (5 subcategories) and 168 from platform B (14 subcategories), 332 analysed after page deletions. Instrument: 10 modified CEWADS criteria (original CEWADS by consensus of 21 Thai regulatory experts; refined by three regulatory experts to the 2021 Thai FDA advertising rules); FDA serial numbers verified against the Thai FDA database; each page scored by a single researcher with no reported inter-rater reliability or blinding; Fisher's exact test for platform comparisons. Limitations acknowledged: the platform algorithm prevented a true random sample; page deletion caused dropout; the FDA database is not always current, which may overestimate prevalence; snapshot of selected subcategories only.
rob.item6_quote: The prevalence of misinformation was assessed based on Thai regulatory criteria by analyzing DS web pages from two popular Thai EM platforms. ... Misinformation prevalence was estimated by the number of web pages with each type of inappropriate information, using 10 Thai food advertising regulatory criteria.
rob.item10_quote: This study counts misinformation as one web page, although duplications were found. The prevalence of overall misinformation and the prevalence of misinformation by format were determined by the number of web pages with the misinformation divided by the total number of sample web pages.
